items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Dickie, Frank, and I knew each other's feeling so well that if anyone of us wanted to play a riff behind a sax solo, which we often did, one would start a riff and the other would pick it up

ctx.x: Sy Oliver, whom I had met not long after I had joined the Scott band and who was still quite young when we played his home town of Zanesville, Ohio, heard us at the Savoy one time (that was before he came to New York with Jimmie Lunceford) and told me that we did not have the best brass section in the business, but that we had the best YOUNG brass section he had ever heard.

Dickie, Frank, and I knew each other's feeling so well that if anyone of us wanted to play a riff behind a sax solo, which we often did, one would start a riff and the other would pick it up and get the feeling of it before one measure had passed, and we played them in harmony and not unison. And a riff was never exactly the same every time although the number was played often.

So Cecil lost the chance of being nationally known because he wanted to make big money but sacrificed the opportunity because he had stolen 45 dollars a week from us for Lord knows how many weeks and he did not want to stop the operation. Both Scott brothers were finished as orchestra leaders.
